sentences.text: Block C had a landing on every floor with a window in it, and the window on the fourth floor did not shut properly, and this was the reason Nadia heard it and the reason she spent four months believing she was the only one who did.
The gap was about the width of two fingers at the top corner of the frame.
In summer it was a good thing.
In November it meant that the fourth-floor landing was the coldest place in the building and that you went up the last flight quickly.

She heard it for the first time on the ninth of November at about twenty past ten, coming up with the recycling, which was not a job she was supposed to be doing at twenty past ten and which she had volunteered for in order to be out of the flat for fourteen minutes.
Her brother had people round.
That was the fourteen minutes.

Her brother was seventeen and had reached the stage of having people round who filled the whole flat with a specific kind of loudness, and Nadia had discovered that the recycling took fourteen minutes if you did it slowly and that nobody ever questioned a person carrying a bag.
Something said her name.
Not her name.
That is the whole of this story and it needs to be right the first time.

It said the other one — the middle one, the one on her documents and nowhere else, the one that had been her grandmother's and her grandmother's grandmother's, three syllables long, with a sound in the middle of it that does not exist in the language she does her homework in.
It said it clearly, at a conversational volume, from somewhere just outside the gap in the window.
Nadia put the bag down on the landing and did not move for a considerable time.
Then she went up to the flat and put the chain on the door and sat on her bed with her coat still on.
Her brother's friends were still in the front room.
Somebody was laughing at something on a phone.
It went on being an entirely ordinary Tuesday on the other side of her bedroom wall for another two hours, and Nadia sat on the bed in her coat for most of it.
She had been at that school for twenty weeks.
She had registered on the first day as Nadia K., because the form had a box for a middle name and she had left it empty, and the woman in the office had not asked.
Nobody in that building, that school, or that city knew the middle name.
Her mother knew it.
Her brother knew it and had been paid, in a formal arrangement involving actual money, not to use it.
And something on the fourth-floor landing had said it out loud into an empty stairwell at twenty past ten at night.
The first three explanations she tried were all sensible and all failed within about a day.
That somebody had seen the documents — but the documents were in a folder in her mother's wardrobe and had not been out of it since the school registration in September.

That her brother had broken the arrangement — but he had not been in the building, he had been at football, and when she checked his phone location history two days later in a way she is not proud of, he had been at football.
That she had misheard something else.
She gave this one four days and a great deal of effort, because it was the one she wanted.
She sat on that landing and tried to make ordinary sounds turn into those three syllables.
It cannot be done.
The middle sound does not exist in this country and there is nothing in a stairwell that makes it.
